name: Vampire facelift

card.summary: A cosmetic treatment that uses platelet-rich plasma from the patient's own blood, with fillers or microneedling, aimed at fuller, smoother, younger-looking skin.
card.note: Infection risk when done in unlicensed settings; a 2024 CDC report linked HIV cases to an unlicensed spa.

quick.overview:
The vampire facelift or vampire facial is an aesthetic treatment based on platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate made by spinning a person's own blood to separate platelets. The plasma is applied or injected into the face, commonly with microneedling, with the goal of smoother, firmer, more even skin.

Proponents say the platelets' growth factors stimulate collagen and cell growth. Wikipedia describes the claimed skin benefits as lacking support from clinical studies, while PRP itself has been studied for other uses such as hair loss and musculoskeletal conditions with mixed results.
quick.how: A clinician draws blood, centrifuges it to produce PRP and applies or injects it into the skin, often after microneedling. Reported effects afterwards are redness, swelling, bruising and tenderness, which providers say usually settle within about two days.
quick.risks: Reported effects are redness, swelling, bruising, numbness and, in some cases, scabbing lasting a week or longer. The main safety concern is infection when equipment is reused: in 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to an unlicensed spa in Albuquerque.

lead: The vampire facelift, also called the vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure and a form of autohemotherapy that combines platelet-rich plasma (PRP) made from the person's own blood with microneedling.[1] Proponents say it stimulates cell growth and collagen and so improves skin health and appearance.[1]

PRP is made by centrifuging blood to remove red cells and keep platelets, which carry growth factors thought to aid healing.[2] In aesthetic medicine it is injected to address wrinkles, lines, blemishes and hair thinning; vampire facials became popular in the 2010s with celebrity endorsement.[2] Kim Kardashian's 2013 Instagram photo of her blood-covered face brought it to wide public attention, and she later said she regretted it and found it painful.[1]

Wikipedia states that the claimed skin benefits are not supported by clinical evidence, and that the main hazard is infection in non-medical settings.[1] In 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among clients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa that reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment, and the New Mexico Department of Health had earlier warned that such businesses could spread bloodborne infections.[1][2]

chain: Apply or inject PRP, often with microneedling
Claimed collagen stimulation and smoother, younger-looking skin
angle.text: Proponents say PRP's growth factors improve skin texture, fine lines and firmness. People use the treatment as an in-clinic skin rejuvenation option.

infobox: PRP use is off-label; preparation devices need FDA clearance

paras: PRP is a concentrate of a patient's own platelets. In the vampire facial the PRP is applied after or alongside microneedling, and the vampire facelift name is also used for PRP injected into facial areas.[1][2]

PRP was used in hematology from the 1970s and cardiac surgery in 1987 and was considered for hair loss by 2006.[2] Cosmetic use grew in the 2010s, and the 2013 Kardashian photo made the treatment widely known.[1][2]

Reported effects include redness, swelling, bruising, tenderness, numbness and pressure at injection sites, with most people recovering in about two days and some reporting scabbing for a week or longer.[1] The 2024 Albuquerque HIV cases illustrate the danger of unsafe practice with reused equipment rather than of PRP itself.[2]
The FDA does not regulate PRP directly, so clinical use is off-label, though the devices that prepare it need clearance.[2]
No studies found for the vampire facelift as a named procedure. PRP generally has been studied for musculoskeletal conditions, wounds and hair loss, with mixed findings.[2]

timeline.event: The term platelet-rich plasma is first used.[2]
Kim Kardashian's Instagram post popularises the vampire facial.[1]
CDC reports three HIV diagnoses linked to an unlicensed Albuquerque spa.[2]
